title: Ang 1298–1311: Guru Arjan in Kanara
hookLine: no enemy, no stranger, on ang 1299
tomorrow: what does Namdev see when he looks in a mirror?

cards: The incoming class group chat is a crowd of strangers posting dorm photos and meal plan questions. Then someone posts a joke about Sikhs and turbans, with a laughing face. A few people react.
Simran types fast, three paragraphs, thumbs shaking. Her cursor sits over send. And the page she read last night, a page into Guru Arjan's hymns in Kanara, says no one is my enemy.

teach.b: Guru Arjan's hymns in Kanara begin on ang 1298, and on ang 1299 comes the line. In paraphrase: I've forgotten all my jealousy of others since I found the company of the holy.
No one is my enemy, no one is bigaana, a stranger; I get along with everyone. Big words for a shaking-thumbs night, and Sikhs read them two ways. Both deserve a hearing.
The first view: this describes a state, a mind so settled in the sangat that hostility drops away. It isn't a rule against speaking.
Sikh tradition honors standing up for others, and a mind with no enemy can still say plainly: that's not okay.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: SPEAK UP, WITHOUT HATE.
teach.b: So answer, but without hate. The second view takes the line as a daily practice before it's a state. If no one is a stranger, the guy who posted the joke isn't either.
He's someone who doesn't know you yet.

teach.h: THE OTHER: NOT IN THE CROWD.
teach.b: So don't answer in the crowd, where everyone performs. Message him alone, or let it pass, and keep your fire. Both views agree on what the line is not.
It isn't nothing matters, and it isn't permission to hate back.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: in the hymn, no stranger comes right after I forgot my jealousy. Letting go of envy comes first. Simran deletes the three paragraphs.
Then she writes one line, and doesn't send it yet.

how: The hymn on ang 1299 is sung in kirtan, and its line about no enemy and no stranger is quoted when Sikhs speak of the sangat and of getting along with all.

games.q: the line on ang 1299 — tap the pairs.
p: a settled state that still speaks up
a daily practice; answer him alone

s: Guru Arjan's 'no enemy' line means nothing anyone does matters
both readings agree it isn't 'nothing matters', and isn't permission to hate back.
in the hymn, forgetting jealousy comes before 'no one is a stranger'
the company of the holy, then no envy, then no enemy and no stranger.
Sikhs all read the 'no enemy' line the same way
some read a settled state that can still speak up; others a daily practice that answers privately.

games.q: your friend thinks 'no enemy' means letting people walk all over you. what's the strongest case for the 'speak up' reading?
o: a mind with no enemy can still say plainly, that's not okay.
'no enemy' was for saints, so ordinary people may fight back.
win every argument, and then nobody is left to be an enemy.
games.why: on the first reading, the line describes a mind with no hostility left, not a rule against speaking. the second reading answers in private. neither says take it, or hate back.

practice: Sit up, and notice where anger lives in you right now: the jaw, the shoulders, the hands. On each out-breath, loosen one of them a little. If someone you're angry with comes to mind, let them stay there while you keep loosening.
